title: Game Theory
objective: After this level you can explain the prisoner's dilemma and why cooperation is hard.
summary: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player does better by betraying whatever the other does, yet both end up worse off. When the game repeats with no known end, cooperation can pay, as tit for tat showed.

cards.headline: Two shops cut prices to steal each other's customers. Both end up poorer.
cards.body: Neither gains a single customer, and both earn smaller profits. Why would two sensible owners do that? Game theory has a famous answer, and it starts in a police station.

cards.headline: The prisoner's dilemma
cards.body: Two suspects are questioned in separate rooms. If both stay silent, each gets a year. If both confess, five years each. If one confesses and the other stays silent, the confessor walks free and the silent one gets 20 years. Work it through: whatever your partner does, confessing leaves you better off. So both confess, and both serve five years instead of one.
cards.callout: Both silent: 1 year each · Both confess: 5 years each

mascot.line: Keep this: each player's best move, taken by both, leaves both worse off.

cards.fact: The prisoner's dilemma was invented before it had any prisoners.
cards.context: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game at the RAND Corporation in 1950. Albert Tucker added the prison story later, to make it easier to explain. The same trap turns up far from any jail: in an arms race, two nations keep buying weapons, neither gains an advantage, and both end up poorer. The price-cutting shops are in it too.

cards.headline: Play again, and trust can pay
cards.body: There's a way out: meet again. When the game repeats and nobody knows which round is last, cooperation can emerge. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments, Anatol Rapoport's tit for tat did famously well: cooperate first, then copy your partner's last move. Axelrod found that every "nice" strategy, one that never betrays first, beat every strategy that wasn't.

cards.headline: The prisoner's dilemma
learned: Betraying is best for each, whatever the other does
Yet both betraying leaves both worse off
Price wars and arms races follow the same logic

questions.prompt: In the classic prisoner's dilemma, if both suspects confess, _____.

options.label: both go free
options.rationale: Only a lone confessor goes free.

options.label: each serves just one year
options.rationale: That's what happens if both stay silent.

options.label: each serves 20 years
options.rationale: Twenty years is for a silent suspect whose partner confesses.

questions.explanation: Both confessing earns five years each, worse than the one year each they'd get by both staying silent.

questions.prompt: Match each person with their part in the story of the prisoner's dilemma.
questions.explanation: Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game in 1950, and Albert Tucker added the prison story. Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments, where Anatol Rapoport's tit for tat did famously well.

questions.prompt: Two rival shops cut prices and neither gains a customer. Since profit is revenue minus costs, why do both earn less?

options.label: Their costs rise whenever their prices fall
options.rationale: Costs aren't what changed; the price did.

options.label: Same customers, lower prices: less revenue
Lower prices are taxed more heavily
Their profits are shared with each other

questions.explanation: Revenue is price times quantity; with the same customers at lower prices, revenue falls while costs stay put.
